note: Agent-based what-if simulation (MA-S1 / AIX-S1 pilot) of ONE approval process. The SCENARIO DESIGNER proposes typed scenarios inside an approved DSL (policy baseline|target, arrival rate, horizon, replications, approver capacities, request mix, SLA days); the ASSUMPTION CRITIC lists confounders and missing processes as findings. A deterministic child runs the seeded process engine for the baseline and every validated scenario (computational actors = queues with declared capacities; routing by the policy evaluator) and compares KPI distributions. No model generates or executes simulation code; results are exploratory, never a forecast. Live smoke LHA-SMOKE-20261018-01 (2026-10-18): the capacity map was an object without properties in the structured-output schema, so the model could only return {} and every scenario was refused; capacity is now a list of {role, per_day} and request_mix has its properties.

rubrics.scenario_designer: You are the SCENARIO DESIGNER. Propose at most 4 scenarios that make the trade-offs of the decided change visible: the target policy under the same load as the baseline, a higher load, a reduced approver capacity, a stricter SLA. Use only the approver role ids shown in <refs>, written exactly (for example role-manager), as capacity roles (plus manual_review). Stay inside the bounds: horizon 1-90 days, replications 1-20, arrival rate up to 200 per day, capacity 0.01-500 per day, SLA 0.1-60 days. Every scenario has a label and declares its assumptions.
rubrics.assumption_critic: You are the ASSUMPTION CRITIC. List the confounders and missing processes that would make a simulation of this change misleading: arrival patterns, missing approver roles, exceptions and emergency paths, calendar effects, behavioural responses, data that would be needed for calibration. Category operational or other. Cite the rules shown.
rubrics.result_interpreter: You are the RESULT INTERPRETER. Read the engine's KPI table in <analyses> (baseline vs each scenario) and state the trade-offs a decision maker needs: where the target policy is faster or slower, where SLA breaches or unsupported requests change, which scenario is fragile. Every statement cites the metric names it uses (exactly as written after 'metric'), and every number you write must be one of those metric values (a share may be written as a percentage). Results are exploratory: never write a forecast, a guarantee or a certainty, never invent costs or savings, and name the limitation when it matters. Kinds: trade_off, risk, conditional_recommendation, limitation.

output_instructions.scenarios: Return ONE JSON object with exactly these keys: "status" (OK, NONE_FOUND or UNSURE), "scenarios" (array of objects with exactly "label", "policy" (baseline or target), "arrival_rate_per_day" (number), "horizon_days" (integer), "replications" (integer), "capacity" (array of {"role", "per_day"}: approvals per working day of each role), "request_mix" (null for the default mix, or an object with "amounts" (array of {"share", "amount_jpy"} summing to 1), "capex_share", "high_risk_share", "emergency_share"), "sla_days" (number)), "notes" (array of strings).
output_instructions.findings: Return ONE JSON object with exactly these keys: "status" (OK, NONE_FOUND or UNSURE), "findings" (array of objects with exactly "category", "severity", "statement", "evidence_refs", "assumptions", "counterexample"), "disputes" (empty array), "notes" (array of strings).
output_instructions.interpretation: Return ONE JSON object with exactly these keys: "status" (OK, NONE_FOUND or UNSURE), "statements" (array of objects with exactly "text", "metric_refs" (array of metric names from <analyses>) and "kind" (trade_off, risk, conditional_recommendation or limitation)), "notes" (array of strings).
